title: Counting Cells Without Being Fooled
endLine: One snapshot misleads; unbiased cell counts sample whole tissue across time.

scenes.tts: How do you count the cells packed inside a whole brain? Older textbooks said glial support cells outnumber neurons ten to one. Solid tissue hides its cells, and one patch can mislead.
scenes.caption: How do you count the cells packed inside a whole brain? Older textbooks said glial support cells outnumber neurons 10 to 1. Solid tissue hides its cells, and one patch can mislead.
scenes.visual: A large translucent brain fills the frame, shimmering with densely packed glowing cells (schematic). A bold question appears: 'How many cells?' A '10 to 1?' tag pulses beside the brain as a small frame scans one patch, unable to see the hidden bulk.
scenes.narration: How do you count the cells packed inside a whole brain? Older textbooks said glial support cells outnumber neurons 10 to 1. Solid tissue hides its cells, and one patch can mislead.

scenes.visual: The glowing brain dims slightly behind the title 'Counting Cells Without Being Fooled' in large high-contrast text, while the cells drift gently (schematic).

scenes.tts: One method keeps tissue intact. Researchers fix a region and cut thin serial sections. Systematic sampling yields unbiased cell numbers from sections, called stereology. Sections also show apoptosis, a regulated death where nuclei condense into dense clumps called pyknotic nuclei.
scenes.caption: One method keeps tissue intact. Researchers fix a region and cut thin serial sections. Systematic sampling yields unbiased cell numbers from sections, called stereology. Sections also show apoptosis, a regulated death where nuclei condense into dense clumps called pyknotic nuclei.
scenes.visual: The brain zooms into a fixed tissue block that slices smoothly into thin serial sections (schematic). A bright sampling frame sweeps across successive slices as a live counter rises, labelled 'Stereology'. One slice enlarges to show a neuron shrinking as its nucleus condenses into a dense dark clump labelled 'Pyknotic nucleus' (schematic).
scenes.narration: One method keeps tissue intact. Researchers fix a region and cut thin serial sections. Systematic sampling yields unbiased cell numbers from sections, called stereology. Sections also show apoptosis, a regulated death where nuclei condense into dense clumps called pyknotic nuclei.

scenes.tts: For a whole brain, slicing every millimetre is slow. Another method dissolves the tissue so nuclei float free. Because this mixture is uniform in every direction, or isotropic, small samples represent the whole. Staining separates neuronal from non-neuronal nuclei: the isotropic fractionator.
scenes.caption: For a whole brain, slicing every millimetre is slow. Another method dissolves the tissue so nuclei float free. Because this mixture is uniform in every direction, or isotropic, small samples represent the whole. Staining separates neuronal from non-neuronal nuclei: the isotropic fractionator.
scenes.visual: The same tissue block drops into a clear tube and dissolves into an even swirling cloud of free nuclei (schematic). Stain washes through, tinting neuronal nuclei cyan and non-neuronal nuclei amber (schematic). A pipette draws samples onto a counting grid, scaling up the whole-brain counter, labelled 'Isotropic fractionator'.
scenes.narration: For a whole brain, slicing every millimetre is slow. Another method dissolves the tissue so nuclei float free. Because this mixture is uniform in every direction, or isotropic, small samples represent the whole. Staining separates neuronal from non-neuronal nuclei: the isotropic fractionator.

scenes.tts: Counts mislead when you confuse density with total number. Density is cells per area or volume. Cortex volume equals height times area. From mouse to human, height gives a factor of two, and area about one thousand. Two times one thousand equals two thousand. Almost all the gain is sideways.
scenes.caption: Counts mislead when you confuse density with total number. Density is cells per area or volume. Cortex volume equals height × area. From mouse to human, height gives a factor of 2, and area about 1,000. 2 × 1,000 = 2,000. Almost all the gain is sideways.
scenes.visual: The tissue view unfolds into mouse and human cortical sheets side by side (schematic). A small square millimetre frame marks density on each. Formula builds on screen as spoken: 'height × area', then '2 × 1,000 = 2,000' (computed from given factors). The human sheet expands far sideways while doubling only modestly in height.
scenes.narration: Counts mislead when you confuse density with total number. Density is cells per area or volume. Cortex volume equals height × area. From mouse to human, height gives a factor of 2, and area about 1,000. 2 × 1,000 = 2,000. Almost all the gain is sideways.

scenes.tts: Time hides a second trap. In Hamburger's raw counts, chick leg motor neurons peak just over twenty thousand. By about day ten of incubation, roughly twelve thousand remain. A low final count is a half-empty bakery shelf: never made, or made then lost. Reliable counts sample whole tissue without bias across time.
scenes.caption: Time hides a second trap. In Hamburger's raw counts, chick leg motor neurons peak just over 20,000. By about day 10 of incubation, roughly 12,000 remain. A low final count is a half-empty bakery shelf: never made, or made then lost. Reliable counts sample whole tissue without bias across time.
scenes.visual: An age scrubber appears beneath the tissue counter. A schematic curve for chick leg motor neurons peaks above '20,000', then drops to '~12,000' at 'Day 10'. The low endpoint bar morphs briefly into a half-empty shelf with two question labels: 'Never made?' and 'Made then lost?'.

scenes.tts: Test that idea. Suppose a mutant ganglion at birth holds far fewer neurons than normal. You can count serial sections at earlier ages too. If neurons were made normally and then lost, how should its curve compare with normal?
scenes.caption: Test that idea. Suppose a mutant ganglion at birth holds far fewer neurons than normal. You can count serial sections at earlier ages too. If neurons were made normally and then lost, how should its curve compare with normal?
scenes.visual: On the age-vs-count graph (schematic), a normal curve rises and settles while a single low dot marks the mutant ganglion at birth. Two dashed paths extend backward to early ages: one matches normal early, one starts low. Question text stays on screen: 'Made then lost: which curve?'
scenes.narration: Test that idea. Suppose a mutant ganglion at birth holds far fewer neurons than normal. You can count serial sections at earlier ages too. If neurons were made normally and then lost, how should its curve compare with normal?

scenes.visual: Hold the question and schematic graph on screen as the two dashed paths pulse gently in alternation for a thinking pause.

scenes.tts: Early on, the mutant matches normal, then drops as dying, pyknotic nuclei appear. If too few were made, it starts low. So researchers count across ages, marking dividing and dying cells. Stop counting too early, and a loss that is merely delayed can look like a lasting excess.
scenes.caption: Early on, the mutant matches normal, then drops as dying, pyknotic nuclei appear. If too few were made, it starts low. So researchers count across ages, marking dividing and dying cells. Stop counting too early, and a loss that is merely delayed can look like a lasting excess.
scenes.visual: The upper dashed path turns solid: the mutant curve tracks normal early, then drops as dark pyknotic markers appear along the slope (schematic). The lower path fades out labelled 'Too few made'. The timeline then extends into adulthood: a second schematic curve stays above normal at an early cut-off line, then falls late to meet normal, tagged 'Delayed, not lasting' (schematic).
scenes.narration: Early on, the mutant matches normal, then drops as dying, pyknotic nuclei appear. If too few were made, it starts low. So researchers count across ages, marking dividing and dying cells. Stop counting too early, and a loss that is merely delayed can look like a lasting excess.

scenes.tts: In 2009, Azevedo and colleagues used the isotropic fractionator on whole human brains. Instead of ten glia per neuron, non-neuronal cells, mostly glia, roughly equalled neurons overall. Glia outnumbered neurons in cerebral cortex; neurons far outnumbered glia in the cerebellum.
scenes.caption: In 2009, Azevedo and colleagues used the isotropic fractionator on whole human brains. Instead of 10 glia per neuron, non-neuronal cells, mostly glia, roughly equalled neurons overall. Glia outnumbered neurons in cerebral cortex; neurons far outnumbered glia in the cerebellum.
scenes.visual: The whole human brain returns, separating into cerebral cortex and cerebellum (schematic). The old '10 to 1' label crosses out and shifts to roughly equal amber and cyan whole-brain bars ('Azevedo and colleagues, 2009'). Amber glia lead in cortex while cyan neurons dominate the cerebellum (schematic).
scenes.narration: In 2009, Azevedo and colleagues used the isotropic fractionator on whole human brains. Instead of 10 glia per neuron, non-neuronal cells, mostly glia, roughly equalled neurons overall. Glia outnumbered neurons in cerebral cortex; neurons far outnumbered glia in the cerebellum.

scenes.tts: In 1980, Rockel and colleagues, and in 2008, Herculano-Houzel and colleagues, counted cortical neurons. Their counts suggest neurons under each square millimetre differ only a few-fold between mouse and human. Area differs about a thousandfold. Extra neurons sit mostly in extra area, not taller columns.
scenes.caption: In 1980, Rockel and colleagues, and in 2008, Herculano-Houzel and colleagues, counted cortical neurons. Their counts suggest neurons under each square millimetre differ only a few-fold between mouse and human. Area differs about a thousandfold. scenes.visual: The mouse and human cortical sheets return ('Rockel et al., 1980; Herculano-Houzel et al., 2008'). Matching square-millimetre columns show neuron counts within a few-fold of each other (schematic), a '~1,000× area' tag appears, while the human sheet unfolds wide to show extra area carrying the extra neurons (schematic).

Extra neurons sit mostly in extra area, not taller columns.

scenes.tts: Counting across ages tracks connections too. In 1997, Peter Huttenlocher and Arun Dabholkar counted synapses, the connections between neurons, in human cortex. Synaptic density peaked and declined later in prefrontal than in auditory cortex, with pruning, the removal of synapses, into adolescence. Measure whole tissue without bias, and follow it through time.

scenes.visual: The age scrubber runs from birth into adolescence beneath the human brain ('Peter Huttenlocher and Arun Dabholkar, 1997'). Two schematic density curves rise and fall: auditory cortex peaks and declines first, while prefrontal cortex peaks later and prunes into adolescence.
